title: Digit Tester
context: Grade 4, the closing topic. An adult sees four rules being memorised. What is actually being taught is what a test does and does not settle. A test answers about the divisor it was run for and about no other, and this chapter teaches four of them and stops, so a number that passes all four has not been fully examined. The printed sharing question turns on exactly that: it shows a number dividing by five and concludes that nothing will be left over when it is shared out, without counting the person doing the sharing, and that is two different mistakes stacked on one line.

writeup.why: Find out what divides a number by looking at it instead of dividing it, and find out what that answer does not cover.
writeup.look: A number laid out one digit to a cell with four test lamps below it, a sum rail underneath and a sharing bay at the side.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Digit Tester' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the tests run against the tests this phase offers, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each lamp is answered and the second fixed at four, which is every test this chapter teaches and no more. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The number stands across the top of the working area as digit cards, one digit to a drawn cell 108 by 124 with 12 between the cells, the row centred at 64,202 and holding up to six of them. A cell is drawn for every digit and a cell holding a zero is drawn and ruled exactly like the rest, at the same size, in the same band, with nothing about it smaller or fainter. The four test lamps stand in a row beneath, each 156 by 108 at 64,366 and spaced 40 apart, marked two, three, five and ten, and a fifth slot of the same size stands beside them at the right, drawn empty and labelled as not taught in this chapter: it can be pressed, it stays dark, and it names what is not known instead of answering. Choosing two, five or ten slides the shutter across the number from the left, leaving only the ones cell showing, and the verdict is given from that one cell. Choosing three stows the shutter and opens the sum rail below the cells, 1086 by 92 at 64,506: every cell has to be dragged down onto it in order, and the rail will not close while any cell is still up. A cell that was passed by is handed back lit with its own digit still showing, zero or not, and the rail totals only what it is actually holding, then runs that total through the same lamp again. The sharing bay stands at the right of the working area, 300 by 400 at 786,202: people are added one at a time as drawn figures, the one handing the things out has a tick box of its own, and no test will run until the count is settled. It then divides by THAT number on a ruled board and sets whatever is left over on the shelf outside the rows at full strength and fully countable. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a digit total, a quotient or a remainder is asked for, and beside them a pair of verdict keys reading yes and not known, so that a child can answer the fifth slot honestly with one press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number built by multiplying is green, anything standing in both lists at once is rose, whatever is left over and any trial that fails is vermilion, the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber, and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a leftover is told by standing outside the rows before it is told by a band, and a list that stops is told by the wall at each end of it and a list that does not by the open edge of the frame. No cell is ever smaller, fainter or narrower for holding a zero, and the rail never closes over a gap. Both of those are one rule with one reason: the page this tool is built from adds the digits of a four digit number and names three of them, and it comes out right, so nothing a child can check would ever have said otherwise.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last number the child tested, its four lamps as they ended, the full sum rail with every cell on it, and the empty slot still dark.

phases.win: the answer lands with the rest of the number still covered by the shutter
phases.does: drops the shutter, reads the one digit still showing and picks a lamp
phases.goal: the ones digit alone decides the tests for two, five and ten
phases.says: Cover everything but the end. Can you still answer? Which digit did it?
phases.check: Is 2,965 divisible by 5? Is it divisible by 10? Look only at its last digit.
phases.feels: the whole number covered up, and the answer still there to be read
phases.hands: Write a long number on the board, seven thousand two hundred and forty-two, and cover all of it with a sheet of paper except the last digit. Ask whether the class can still say if it divides by two. Do it again for one thousand and twenty-five with the test for five, and for eighty-nine thousand six hundred and thirty with the test for ten. Each time, uncover the number afterwards and divide it out to see that the test told the truth.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which cell is the ones cell? Second rung, the phase's: what is standing in it? Third rung: the number is cut to two cells, the shutter drops, and the child answers from the one cell left showing. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the rule for three is the one that felt like a method, with every cell coming down onto the rail and the zeros counted in like the rest, and a method that was hard to learn gets reached for first whatever the lamp says.
wrong.move: adds the digits up to test a number for two, because adding the digits is the rule that took the most learning.
wrong.screen: the shutter slides across and leaves only the ones cell showing, and the verdict is given from that one cell while the sum rail stays stowed and closed. The total the child built stays where it was written, and the lamp for three lights beside the lamp for two so that the rule and the test it belongs to are drawn together. Nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: reading, writing and saying a number all start at the left, and the ones place is the last thing a number gets round to.
wrong.move: reads the first digit instead of the last, because a number is read from the left hand end.
wrong.screen: the cells are named from the RIGHT hand end, ones first, with each name written under its own cell, and the shutter is drawn closing from the left so that the cell still showing is plainly the one the test was chosen for. The number is then divided out in full on the board beside it, and the child's verdict stays in the slot with the leading digit still lit where they were looking.

phases.screen: a long number with the shutter ready and three of the lamps lit
phases.soWhat: The ones digit alone settles the tests for two, for five and for ten.

phases.win: the rail closes only when every cell has come down, and the total runs through the test
phases.does: drags each cell down onto the rail in order, zeros and all, then tests the total
phases.goal: every digit goes into the total, zeros included
phases.says: Take every card down, even the empty looking ones. Leave none out.
phases.check: Test 80,690 for divisibility by 3, writing down every digit including both zeros.
phases.feels: a zero adds nothing, and skipping it loses everything that comes after it
phases.hands: Write 6405 on squared paper with one digit to a square, all four of them, and add the four together. The page prints this same sum with only three numbers in it. Find the digit the page left out, say what it adds to the total, and say why the answer came out right anyway. Then do the same on 80,690, where two zeros have to be written down and the digits either side of them are the ones that get lost if a cell is skipped.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which cell is still up? Second rung, the phase's: how many cells does this number have altogether? Third rung: the number is cut to three cells with a zero in the middle and the child brings all three down in order. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the total does come out right, so nothing the child can check ever says the step was wrong, and the printed demonstration of this very rule does exactly the same thing on the same number.
wrong.move: leaves the zero out of the total, because a zero adds nothing to it.
wrong.screen: the rail will not close and the skipped cell is handed back lit, with its zero drawn at full size where it stands and the gap on the rail left open at its full width. Once every cell has come down the total is written and sent back up through the lamp. The same run is then laid on a five digit number holding two zeros, where the cells either side of them are the ones a skipping finger takes with it.

wrong.why: the adding is the new work and it is the part that took effort, so it feels like the thing that was being asked for.
wrong.move: adds the digits, writes the total and stops there, reporting the total as the answer.
wrong.screen: the total the rail built rises back up into the cells as a number in its own right and the lamp for three lights again above it, asking to be pressed a second time. The first total stays drawn where the rail wrote it, and the verdict that comes out of the second press is written under the number the child started from.

phases.screen: a number holding two zeros with the sum rail open and empty below it
phases.soWhat: Every digit goes into the total for the test for three, zeros included.

phases.win: the empty slot stays dark and named, and the child says nothing is known about it
phases.does: asks the empty slot a question and is shown it was never taught
phases.goal: four tests are taught here and they settle nothing else
phases.says: It passed every test here. Now tell me about four. Can you?
phases.check: 1,050 and 1,080 both pass every test in this chapter. Which of the two divides by 4, and what did the tests tell you about that?
phases.feels: four lamps lit, and the slot beside them still dark
phases.hands: Write 1,050 and 1,080 on the board and run this chapter's four tests on both of them. Both pass all four. Now ask the class which of the two divides by four, take a vote, and then divide each of them by four and count what is left. Finish by asking what the four tests had actually told them about four, and accept only the answer that they had told them nothing.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which tests has this chapter taught you? Second rung, the phase's: is the number you are being asked about one of them? Third rung: the lamps are cut to two and the child is asked about a third divisor and presses the not known key. The verdict keys stay open.

wrong.why: six really is two threes, so a number that three goes into looks as though it is most of the way to six already, and no test on the page contradicts it.
wrong.move: says a number that passed the test for three must divide by six as well, because six is made out of two and three.
wrong.screen: the fifth slot lights and stays dark beside the four lamps. The number is divided by six on the ruled board, its rows drawn and three set on the leftover shelf outside them at full strength, and the lamp for two is pressed on the same number and does not fill. The child's claim stays in the answer slot with the division standing under it.

wrong.why: four lamps full look like a finished job, and nothing on the page ever says how many tests there are altogether.
wrong.move: treats a number that has passed every lamp on the stage as a number that has been fully examined.
wrong.screen: both numbers that passed all four are divided by four side by side on one board, one coming out with the shelf empty and the other leaving two standing outside the rows at full strength. The four lamps stay full above both of them the whole time, and the fifth slot stays dark and named. Nothing is marked either way.

phases.screen: a number that has passed all four lamps, with the empty slot beside them
phases.soWhat: A test answers for the number you tested by and for no other, so this chapter's four tests settle four things and nothing else.
phases.concept: What the tests do not cover

phases.win: the count changes, the test runs on the new number and any leftover stands outside the rows
phases.does: counts the people, ticks the one handing them out, then tests by that number
phases.goal: count everyone sharing, including the person handing the things out
phases.says: Count everyone who is sharing. Have you counted the one handing them out?
phases.check: You invite 5 friends, you have 24 buns, and you are eating one share yourself. How many are sharing, and will any be left?
phases.feels: the person holding the tray is sharing too
phases.hands: Act it out. Sit six children in a circle with fifty counters in the middle and deal them out one at a time, round and round, until nobody can have another. Count what is left. Then take one child out of the circle and do the whole thing again with the same fifty. Ask what changed, and why the person holding the tray has to be counted before anybody divides anything.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many friends were asked? Second rung, the phase's: is anybody sharing who has not been counted yet? Third rung: the bay is cut to a small party, the child counts the figures, ticks the box and reads the new count. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the number of friends is the number the question says out loud, and the person holding the tray is not usually counted among the guests; the printed page does exactly this and states the conclusion flatly.
wrong.move: tests fifty by five, because five friends were invited, and concludes that none will be left.
wrong.screen: the sharing bay counts the people out one at a time as drawn figures, and the tick box for the one handing them out is still empty and lights. Ticking it changes the count, the division runs again on the new count, and two are set on the shelf outside the rows at full strength. The first division stays drawn beside it with the number it was run for written under it.

wrong.why: one test has been passed and a passed test feels like a finished answer, so the divisor it was run for stops being part of what was shown.
wrong.move: shows that fifty divides by five and takes that as settling whether any will be left, whoever ends up sharing.
wrong.screen: both divisions are drawn on the same board, one under the other: fifty into five rows with the shelf beside it empty, and fifty into six rows with two standing outside at full strength. Each board is labelled with the number it was run for, and the question is read again above them with the words how many are sharing lit.

phases.screen: the sharing bay with the friends counted and the host box still unticked
phases.soWhat: Count everyone who is sharing before you choose a divisor, and remember the test answers only for the divisor you chose.
phases.concept: Testing for the right number of people

writeup.delight: The second phase, at the moment a cell is skipped. The rail does not shut and nothing is marked: the cell that was passed by lifts a little where it stands, lights, and its digit is drawn larger for a beat, zero and all, while the cells that did come down stay lying on the rail in exactly the order they arrived. The gap on the rail where that cell belongs stays open at its full width, so the missing one is a hole in the line rather than a line that closed up neatly behind it. Bring it down and the rail shuts, the total is written, and the total goes straight back up through the lamp.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a long number stands across the top in its cells with the shutter drawn back at the left and three of the four lamps lit. On the second a number holding two zeros stands in its cells, every cell drawn the same size whatever is in it, with the sum rail open and empty underneath and the shutter stowed. On the third a number that has already passed all four lamps stands in the cells with the four lamps full and the fifth slot beside them drawn and dark. On the fourth the sharing bay is open at the side with the invited friends counted out as drawn figures and the tick box for the one handing the things out still empty. The running count at the top left holds the tests run against the tests this phase offers, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the ones cell, or the leftmost cell still waiting above the rail, or the dark fifth slot, or the empty tick box, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how much of the number has to be looked at. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number up to six digits, all four lamps live, with the sum rail open and the sharing bay beside it. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on reading the ones digit, adding every digit for three, saying what the tests leave unanswered, and testing by the right number of people.
voiceLines: A number laid out, one digit to a cell, and four lamps underneath it.
Cover everything but the end. Can you still answer? Which digit did it?
Take every card down, even the empty looking ones. Leave none out.
It passed every test here. Now tell me about four. Can you?
Count everyone who is sharing. Have you counted the one handing them out?
A new number in the cells. Which lamp are you going to choose?
Free play. Any number in the cells, all four lamps live, the sharing bay beside them.
Bring every cell down again, and leave none of them up there.
Four tests run, every cell counted in, and one slot that stayed dark.

observations.why: Ten, and five and two inside it, are settled by what stands in the ones place alone.
observations.soWhat: For those three tests, nothing but the last digit matters.
observations.observe: For two, for five and for ten the whole number was covered and the answer was still available.

observations.why: A zero adds nothing to the total, so skipping one never shows up in the answer and the habit survives.
observations.soWhat: Every digit comes down, zeros included, and a total built from some of the digits is not the test.
observations.observe: The rail refused to close while one cell was still up, even when that cell held a zero.

observations.why: This chapter teaches four tests, and none of them is about any other divisor.
observations.soWhat: A test answers for the number you tested by and for no other, so passing all four is not being fully examined.
observations.observe: A number that passed all four lamps left the fifth slot exactly as dark as it began.

observations.why: The person handing the things out is sharing too, so the divisor was wrong before the test was ever run.
observations.soWhat: Count everyone who is sharing before you choose what to divide by.
observations.observe: The count in the sharing bay changed the moment the tick box was ticked, and the leftover changed with it.

source_tool.description: A number arrives across the top of the stage as digit cards, one digit to a cell, with the cells drawn whether the digit in them is a zero or not. Four test lamps stand below, marked two, three, five and ten, and a fifth slot is drawn beside them and plainly labelled as not taught here, so the limit of the chapter is a thing on the stage rather than a sentence nobody read. Choosing two, five or ten drops a shutter across the number that leaves only the ones digit showing, because nothing else in the number matters for those three. Choosing three opens a sum rail underneath instead, and every cell has to be dragged down onto it, zeros included: the rail will not close over a gap, and a skipped cell is handed back lit with its own zero still in it. The total then runs through the same test again. A sharing bay sits at the side and asks who is sharing before it will run anything. People are added one at a time, the person handing the things out is a tick box of its own, and only when the count is settled does the bay test by THAT number and draw whatever is left over outside the rows.
source_tool.art_direction: Digit cells, four lamps, one sum rail / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: trays of countable things, ruled rows on a board, a ladder of rungs with one trial to a rung, a pen with a wall at each end, a track of equal steps, cards that turn over, and two rings of cord that overlap.

Equal groups are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a row is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are in it, and the rows are kept apart by a drawn wall or a plain gap and never by colour alone.

Whatever is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the rows, on the same surface, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never crossed out, never tucked under a row and never left to be guessed from a gap. The leftover is the reason a trial failed, so it is the last thing any stage may hide.

A list of factors is drawn penned in between one and the number itself, with both ends of the run plainly stopped by a wall or a final post, so the list can be seen to end. A list of multiples is drawn running from the number away to the right, and the track carrying it leaves the frame with no end mark and no last step drawn, so the list can be seen not to end. The two never run the same way on one stage.

A run of trials is drawn unbroken. Every whole number from one up to the last one tried keeps its own rung or row, in order, with none left out, and a trial that fails is drawn and marked as a failure rather than dropped.
Where the digits of a number are added, every digit sits in its own cell, zeros included, and a cell holding a zero is drawn and counted in rather than left out of the line.
Nothing the child is asked to count one at a time comes to more than twenty things in one group. A larger quantity is a ruled array of identical tiles or a written numeral, never a loose heap.
A list is told apart by the wall or the open edge at its end first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a counter or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. A number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number that is built by multiplying is green, and anything standing in both lists at once is rose, and those three hold in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Whatever is left over, and any trial that fails, is vermilion; the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber; and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. All of that holds in greyscale, because a failed trial is told apart by the leftover drawn outside its row before it is told apart by colour, and a factor list is told apart from a list of multiples by the wall at each end of it before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Bring every cell down again, and leave none of them up there.
voice.onNext: A new number in the cells. Which lamp are you going to choose?
voice.opening: A number laid out, one digit to a cell, and four lamps underneath it.
voice.onFinish: Four tests run, every cell counted in, and one slot that stayed dark.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any number in the cells, all four lamps live, the sharing bay beside them.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: What the tests do not cover
Testing for the right number of people

placement.where: After a handful of numbers have been sorted into labelled trays by hand and a few of them checked by actually dividing. The tool is what refuses to close a digit sum while a cell is still up, zeros included, which is the exact slip the printed demonstration makes and that no written page can catch.

answer_key.rule: A number is divisible by 2 when its ones digit is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8, by 5 when its ones digit is 5 or 0, and by 10 when its ones digit is 0. For those three, nothing but the last digit matters. A number is divisible by 3 when the total of its digits is divisible by 3, and every digit goes into that total, zeros included, because a zero adds nothing but skipping one loses whatever comes after it. This chapter teaches those four tests and no others, so nothing here settles 4, 6, 8 or 9. A test answers about the number you tested by and about no other, so before choosing a divisor, count everyone who is sharing, including the person handing the things out.
answer_key.wrong: The cells all light again and the sum rail reopens with every cell, zeros included, waiting to be dragged down in order, and the sharing bay reopens with the people counted out one at a time. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: For the test for 2, nothing but the ones digit matters, so the rest can be covered.
The ones digit of 4,386 is 6, and 6 is one of 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8.
So 4386 is divisible by 2, and dividing it out gives 2193.
items.answer: Yes, because its ones digit is 6
items.question: Is 4,386 divisible by 2? Look only at the end of it.
items.checkpoint: The ones digit alone decides the tests for two, for five and for ten.
items.misconception: Adding up all the digits for the test for two, which is the rule for three.

steps: The digits are 4, 0, 6, 0 and 8, and both zeros come down onto the rail with the rest.
They add to 18, which 3 divides exactly.
So 40608 is divisible by 3, and dividing it out gives 13536.
items.answer: Yes, because the digits add to 18 and 3 divides 18
items.question: Test 40,608 for divisibility by 3, writing every digit down.
items.checkpoint: Every digit goes into the total for the test for three, zeros included.
items.misconception: Adding 4, 6 and 8 only, because the zeros look as though they can be left out.

steps: This chapter teaches four tests, for 2, 3, 5 and 10, and no others.
None of those four says anything about whether 4 divides the number.
It might divide by 4 and it might not, and nothing shown here settles it.
items.question: A number passes the tests for 2, for 3, for 5 and for 10. What do you now know about 4?
items.checkpoint: A test answers for the number you tested by and for no other.
items.misconception: Treating a number that passes every test on the page as a number that has been fully examined.

steps: Count everyone who is sharing: 4 friends and the boy himself makes 5.
So the number to test by is 5, not 4, and 35 divided by 5 is 7 with nothing over.
Testing by 4 instead would have said 3 were left, which answers a question nobody asked.
items.answer: Five people are sharing, counting the boy, and none will be left
items.question: A boy asks 4 friends to his party and has 35 laddoos to share out equally. Who is sharing, and will any be left?
items.checkpoint: Count everyone who is sharing, including the person handing them out, before choosing a divisor.
items.misconception: Dividing by the number of friends and forgetting the person handing the food round.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Is 7,314 divisible by 5?
items.final_answer: No. Its ones digit is 4, and a number divisible by 5 ends in 5 or 0

items.question: Is 6,470 divisible by 10?
items.final_answer: Yes. Its ones digit is 0, and 6470 divided by 10 is 647

items.question: Add every digit of 3,105 and say whether 3 divides it.
items.final_answer: The digits add to 9, so yes; 3105 divided by 3 is 1035

items.question: Test 50,073 for divisibility by 3.
items.final_answer: Yes. Every digit counts, so 5 and 0 and 0 and 7 and 3 add to 15, which 3 divides

items.question: Which of 2,946 and 2,945 is divisible by 2, and which by 5?
items.final_answer: 2946 divides by 2 because it ends in 6, and 2945 divides by 5 because it ends in 5

items.question: A number ends in 0 and its digits add to 12. Which of this chapter's four tests does it pass?
items.final_answer: All four: by 2, by 5 and by 10 from its ones digit, and by 3 because 3 divides 12

items.question: A child shows that 7,005 divides by 3 and then says it must divide by 6 as well. What is wrong?
items.final_answer: The chapter has no test for 6, and 7005 does not divide by 6 at all, because it is odd. A test answers for the number tested by and no other

items.question: A cook has 70 rolls and asks 7 friends to share them, taking a share himself. He tests 70 by 7 and says none will be left. What has he missed?
items.final_answer: Himself. With him there are 8 sharing, and 70 divided by 8 is 8 with 6 left over

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: lays the number out one digit to a cell, with a cell drawn for every zero
offers the tests for two, three, five and ten, and no others
stands beside the lamps and names what this chapter does not test
covers everything but the ones digit for the tests for two, five and ten
takes every digit down in order and will not close over a gap
hands back a cell that was skipped, with its zero still showing
counts everyone who is sharing, including the person handing them out
draws whatever is left over outside the rows, countable and at full strength

teaching_notes: Sort real number cards into four labelled trays by hand before the tool is opened, and then check two or three of them by actually dividing, so the tests are seen to be true rather than taken on trust. Cover the number with a hand for the first few tests for two, five and ten, leaving only the last digit showing, and ask whether the answer is still available. It is, and that surprises them. For the test for three, insist that every digit comes down, zeros included, and say why out loud: a zero adds nothing to the total, but a child who skips a zero learns to skip, and the next number has something else in that place. The printed demonstration of this rule adds three of a four digit number's digits, and the very next exercise hands over a five digit number with two zeros in the middle, so the habit is tested immediately. The last phase is the one to leave time for. Count the sharers out loud, one person at a time, and always ask who is missing from the count. The answer is usually the person holding the tray. Then ask what the test actually proved, and accept only an answer that names the divisor it was run for.
generation_prompt: Build a divisibility tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A number up to six digits long sits across the top as digit cards, one digit to a drawn cell, with a cell drawn for every zero exactly as for every other digit. Four test lamps below are marked two, three, five and ten, and a fifth slot beside them is drawn empty and labelled as not taught in this chapter; it can be tapped and stays dark, naming what is not known rather than answering. Choosing two, five or ten slides a shutter across the number leaving only the ones digit visible, and the verdict is given from that digit alone. Choosing three opens a sum rail beneath the cells; every cell must be dragged down onto the rail in order, and the rail refuses to close while any cell is still up, lighting the skipped cell with its digit, including a zero, still showing. The rail totals what it holds and runs the total through the same test. A sharing bay at the side counts the people sharing one at a time as drawn figures, with a separate tick box for the person handing the things out, and will not run a test until the count is settled; it then divides by that count and draws whatever is left over outside the rows at full strength and fully countable. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Lay the number out, one digit to a cell. For two, five and ten, cover everything but the last digit. For three, bring every cell down onto the rail, zeros and all, and test the total. Before you test a sharing question, count everyone who is sharing.
